May be taken with or without food; avoid grapefruit
Can cause fetal harm - contraindicated; use effective contraception
Do not breastfeed during and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose
No adjustment in mild-moderate; start 400 mg in severe impairment
No adjustment in mild; start 400 mg in moderate-severe impairment
Avoid excess - both alcohol and ribociclib can stress the liver

summary: Ribociclib is an oral, selective inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (CDK4/6) used with endocrine therapy to treat hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer (and in the adjuvant setting for early breast cancer). By blocking CDK4/6 it prevents retinoblastoma-protein phosphorylation, arresting tumour cells in G1 phase. Two distinctive safety signals dominate its label: dose- and concentration-dependent QT-interval prolongation (requiring ECG and electrolyte monitoring) and hepatobiliary toxicity (transaminase elevations, requiring liver function monitoring). Neutropenia is the most common dose-limiting hematologic effect.
indications: HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer in combination with an aromatase inhibitor as initial endocrine-based therapy (pre/peri/postmenopausal women and men)
HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer in combination with fulvestrant as initial or after disease progression on endocrine therapy
Adjuvant treatment of HR-positive, HER2-negative stage II/III early breast cancer at high risk of recurrence, in combination with an aromatase inhibitor

dosage.d: 600 mg (3 x 200 mg tablets) PO once daily, 21 days on then 7 days off
dosage.n: Given with an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant; with fulvestrant, premenopausal/perimenopausal women also receive an LHRH agonist
Reduce for neutropenia, QTc prolongation, hepatotoxicity per label
Discontinue if unable to tolerate 200 mg

dosage.c: Severe renal or moderate-severe hepatic impairment
dosage.n: No starting dose change for mild-moderate renal or mild hepatic impairment

admin: Take tablets whole at about the same time each day, preferably in the morning; do not chew, crush or split
Take with or without food; avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice
Do not take a damaged, broken or split tablet
If a dose is vomited or missed, do not replace it - take the next dose at the usual time
Obtain a baseline ECG and electrolytes; do not start if QTcF is over 450 ms
moa: Ribociclib selectively inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6. CDK4/6 complexed with cyclin D phosphorylates the retinoblastoma protein (Rb), releasing E2F transcription factors that drive cell-cycle progression from G1 into S phase. By inhibiting CDK4/6, ribociclib prevents Rb phosphorylation and arrests cancer cells in G1, blocking proliferation; in HR-positive breast cancer this is synergistic with endocrine therapy that suppresses estrogen-driven cyclin D expression.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ribociclib or excipients
relative: Baseline QTcF over 450 ms or long QT syndrome
Concurrent QT-prolonging drugs or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Active or recent serious infection (neutropenia risk)
monitor: Signs of severe cutaneous adverse reactions or interstitial lung disease

preg: Based on its mechanism and animal data, ribociclib can cause fetal harm. It is contraindicated in pregnancy. Verify pregnancy status before starting, and women of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose.
lact: It is not known whether ribociclib passes into human milk, but it is present in the milk of lactating animals. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed child, advise against breastfeeding during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the final dose.
renal: No starting-dose adjustment is needed for mild or moderate renal impairment. For severe renal impairment, a reduced starting dose of 400 mg once daily is recommended.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed for mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A). For moderate to severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B and C), reduce the starting dose to 400 mg once daily. Hepatobiliary toxicity also requires monitoring of liver function during treatment.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit) markedly raise ribociclib exposure - avoid; if unavoidable reduce ribociclib dose
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, St John's wort) lower ribociclib exposure - avoid
Other QT-prolonging drugs (certain antiarrhythmics, methadone, ondansetron at high IV dose, some antipsychotics/antibiotics) - additive torsades risk; avoid
Sensitive CYP3A4 substrates with narrow therapeutic index (e.g., some statins, fentanyl, midazolam) - ribociclib inhibits CYP3A4 and raises their levels
moderate: Drugs that affect electrolytes (diuretics) - correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia to limit QT risk
Tamoxifen combination increases QT prolongation (not recommended)
minor: Proton pump inhibitors may modestly alter absorption
interactions.food: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibition increases exposure); may otherwise be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid heavy alcohol use because of additive hepatotoxicity risk
interactions.diagnostics: Obtain baseline and on-treatment ECG (QTcF) and electrolytes; monitor CBC and LFTs to detect neutropenia and hepatotoxicity

serious: QT-interval prolongation (risk of torsades de pointes)
Hepatobiliary toxicity (marked transaminase elevations, hepatic injury)
Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, DRESS, toxic epidermal necrolysis)
emergency: Syncope or torsades de pointes from marked QT prolongation
Acute dyspnea/hypoxia from interstitial lung disease

monitoring: ECG at baseline, around day 14 of cycle 1, at the start of cycle 2, and as clinically indicated; do not start or hold if QTcF over 450-480 ms per protocol
Serum potassium, magnesium, calcium and phosphorus - correct before and during therapy
Complete blood count before starting, every 2 weeks for the first 2 cycles, then before each subsequent cycle
Liver function tests before starting, every 2 weeks for the first 2 cycles, then at the start of each of the next 4 cycles, then as indicated
Pulmonary symptoms (cough, dyspnea) and skin reactions
counsel: Take three tablets once daily at the same time, for 3 weeks on and 1 week off; swallow whole and avoid grapefruit
Report fainting, palpitations, dizziness, or a known heart-rhythm problem - this drug can affect heart rhythm
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, or right-sided abdominal pain (liver problems)
Report fever, chills, or signs of infection promptly, and any new or worsening cough or breathlessness
Use effective contraception and do not breastfeed during and for 3 weeks after treatment; report any severe skin rash, blistering, or mouth sores immediately
pk: Steady state reached in about 8 days of daily dosing
Plasma peak approximately 1-4 hours after oral dosing
Store at 20-25 C (excursions 15-30 C permitted); keep in original packaging
pearls: Two signature toxicities define ribociclib: concentration-dependent QT prolongation (mandating ECG/electrolyte monitoring) and hepatobiliary toxicity (mandating LFT monitoring) - check both before each relevant timepoint
Do not start if baseline QTcF exceeds 450 ms and correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia first
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (including grapefruit) sharply raise levels - avoid; ribociclib itself inhibits CYP3A4 and can raise levels of co-administered substrates
Neutropenia is the commonest dose-limiting effect - it is generally rapidly reversible with dose interruption/reduction
Combination with tamoxifen is not recommended due to greater QT prolongation; pair with an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant
missed: If you miss a dose or vomit after taking it, do NOT take an extra dose to make up. Skip the missed dose and take your next scheduled dose at the usual time the following day. Tell your care team if you frequently miss or vomit doses.
overdose: Overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, fatigue and an increased risk of QT prolongation and hematologic and hepatic toxicity. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with cardiac monitoring (ECG for QTc), correction of electrolytes, and general symptomatic and supportive care; consider hemodialysis is unlikely to be useful given high protein binding.
